title: Document rootless bind-mount access through an unmapped parent
body:
A user asked in https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/discussions/29443 why rootless Podman let him bind-mount a directory under `/etc/letsencrypt`, owned by `certbot:certbot` and mode 750, when his user is not in that group. The answer is in how the user namespace maps IDs, and the tutorial never says so. I isolated the rule on three directories of my own.

All three parents are mode 700, and the child under each is mounted with `podman run --rm -v /tmp/<parent>/child:/mnt alpine echo ok`. With the parent owned by `0:0` it fails with `Error: statfs /tmp/t_root/child: permission denied`. Owned by `300000:300000`, above my range, it fails the same way. Owned by `100999:100999`, inside `jmrplens:100000:65536`, it prints `ok`. `podman unshare ls -ldn` shows why: the first two parents are owned by 65534 inside the namespace, the third by 1000. `--userns=keep-id` changes none of them. This is podman 5.4.2 on Debian, the same version as the reporter.

The rule is in user_namespaces(7), section "Unmapped user and group IDs": an unmapped user ID is converted to the overflow user ID, 65534 by default. A capability in a user namespace only permits privileged operations on resources that namespace governs, so root in the namespace holds no DAC override over a file whose owner is unmapped. The parent's mode is then enforced as it would be for any other user. A parent owned inside the subuid range is mapped, the override applies, and mode 700 is bypassed.

The "Using volumes" section covers the ID shift for files created inside the container and the `--userns=keep-id` advice, and stops there. The words "unmapped" and "overflow" appear nowhere under `docs/`. This adds one subsection at the end of that section with the two outcomes, the `podman unshare` check, and a line tying the range-overlap hazard back to the impersonation warning the `/etc/subuid` section already gives. There is no issue for this one, so the commit carries the discussion URL instead of a `Fixes:` line. Documentation only, no code and no test changes.

On `make validatepr`: it builds the binaries and lints the Go tree, which this change does not touch, so I did not run the full target. The pre-commit hooks it carries (end-of-file, trailing whitespace, mixed line endings, codespell with the repo's `.codespellrc`) pass on the file, and `hack/commit-subject-check.sh` passes on the commit.

title: Use pasta for published-port forwarding on user-defined (bridge) networks, so that client source addresses are preserved

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

body:
### Feature request description

In rootless mode with a user-defined network, Podman already starts pasta to connect the rootless netns to the host - but explicitly disables its port forwarding (-t none -u none -T none -U none). Published ports are instead forwarded by rootlessport (rootlesskit), which SNATs the connection and therefore loses the client source address.

Since pasta is already running for exactly this netns, and preserving source addresses is one of its design goals: 
could the published-port forwarding be handed to pasta for bridge networks as well?

Current behaviour — Traefik rootless on a user-defined network, publishing 80/443. Its access log records the internal bridge address for a request that came from a public IPv4:
 {"ClientAddr":"10.89.1.7:57110","ClientHost":"10.89.1.7","RequestHost":"git.example.com","RequestMethod":"GET","DownstreamStatus":200,"RouterName":"gitea@file"}

pasta runs with forwarding off, rootlesskit does the work:

/usr/bin/pasta --config-net --pid …/rootless-netns-conn.pid --dns-forward 169.254.1.1 \
    -t none -u none -T none -U none --no-map-gw --quiet --netns …/rootless-netns \
    --map-guest-addr 169.254.1.2                                                                                                      

podmgr 44770  rootlessport
podmgr 44778  rootlessport-child                                                                                                    

This is not cosmetic for a reverse proxy. With every request appearing to come from one internal address:

- access logs cannot serve as an audit record - every request looks identical
- X-Forwarded-For set by the proxy carries the internal address, so all backends behind it inherit the wrong value
- per-client rate limiting silently becomes global rate limiting  
- authentication event logs (e.g. Keycloak login events) record the wrong IP                                                        
- fail2ban-style blocking is impossible, as there is nothing distinguishable to ban

The failure mode is silent: everything appears to work and the values are simply wrong.                                           



### Suggest potential solution

Hand published-port forwarding to pasta for user-defined networks as well, instead of using rootlesskit.

pasta is already running for the rootless netns and preserving source addresses is one of its design goals, so the mechanism is present - it is just started with -t none -u none -T none -U none and the ports are routed around it.

If replacing rootlesskit unconditionally is undesirable (rootlesskit is faster, which is presumably why it is the default), an opt-in would already help: a containers.conf setting, or extending the existing port_handler= option so that it also applies to netavark bridge networks rather than only to slirp4netns-backed ones.


### Have you considered any alternatives?

Yes, four - none of which keeps both source addresses and container-name resolution, which is the combination a reverse proxy needs.

- port_handler=slirp4netns - documented in containers.conf as the source-address-preserving handler, but it applies when slirp4netns is the network. It does not apply to a netavark bridge inside the rootless netns.
- --network=pasta - preserves source addresses, but gives up the bridge and aardvark-dns name resolution that a multi-container proxy setup depends on.
- --network=host for the proxy - works, but then every backend has to publish a port on the host loopback and service discovery by container name is lost.
- running the proxy rootful - works, but a rootful proxy cannot reach rootless containers, so in practice the whole stack has to move to rootful, which defeats the purpose of the rootless setup. 

### Additional context

title: compat API: accept inline seccomp profiles

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Change to remote API; merits scrutiny

body:
Docker clients send the seccomp profile JSON itself in HostConfig.SecurityOpt (the docker CLI reads the profile file client-side and inlines it). The compat API treated the value as a path to a profile file, so container create failed with "file name too long". This breaks docker-compat tooling that passes seccomp profiles through the socket, like Nextcloud AIO and forgejo-runner.

Add a SeccompProfile field to specgen for inline profile content, next to the existing SeccompProfilePath, as requested in review of the earlier PR that tried to fix this (#28985). The compat create handler extracts inline profiles (values starting with "{") from SecurityOpt and sets the new field. Path-based values and "unconfined" keep their current meaning, and duplicate seccomp options resolve last-one-wins, like docker.

The profile loader in specgen/generate loads the inline profile directly, the two fields are validated as mutually exclusive, and inline profiles round-trip through inspect's SecurityOpt like they do with docker.

Fixes: #27710

title: Fix build --secret leaving plaintext next to the context

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Change to remote API; merits scrutiny

body:
## Summary

`processSecrets` renamed each build secret into the **parent of the build context** and never deleted it. For local-API / `podman machine` builds that parent is a user directory, so a successful `podman build --secret` left `podman-build-secret-*` next to the context (mode 0600 plaintext).

Secrets are still moved out of the context so `COPY` cannot pick them up, but they now go under `parse.GetTempDir()` and are removed by the existing `temporaryFiles` cleanup when the build finishes.

## Test plan

- [x] `go test -tags 'exclude_graphdriver_btrfs containers_image_openpgp' ./pkg/api/handlers/compat/ -count=1 -run TestProcessSecretsDoesNotLeavePlaintextInContextParent`
- [ ] Reproduce issue steps: build from a third directory with `--secret`, confirm no `podman-build-secret-*` remains in the context parent

Fixes #29687

title: sqlite state DB corrupts under sustained container churn: "database disk image is malformed"

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

body:
### Issue Description

Podman’s sqlite state database (`/var/lib/containers/storage/db.sql`) became corrupted on two independent production VMs on 2026-09-04, with an identical and unusual damage signature. After onset, every state-changing operation (container create/remove/wait) fails with `database disk image is malformed` until the store is wiped; the corruption survives reboot.

Both hosts run a synthetic-monitoring workload: a runner drives the rootful podman API service (socket-activated) with sustained container churn: ~23 distinct images, ~15 containers in flight, ~1.9 container lifecycles/second, ~29 write transactions/second on the state DB (change-counter delta over uptime), plus conmon-spawned `podman container cleanup` processes writing to the same DB.

- **Host 1:** corrupted 8.2 hours after first boot, 54,858 container lifecycles completed cleanly before the first failure.
- **Host 2** (its replacement, same zone, different workload release tag): corrupted 1 hour 38 minutes after first boot.

**Forensics (from copies of both db.sql files):**

- `PRAGMA integrity_check` returns exactly one finding on each: `Freelist: size is 0 but should be 4` (host 1) / `size is 0 but should be 3` (host 2). All tables enumerate normally.
- Page-1 header bytes 32–39: first-freelist-trunk-page pointer = 0 (empty freelist) while the adjacent freelist-page-count field = 4 (resp. 3). The two adjacent fields each hold a valid value from a *different* consistent state. A torn write or bit flip cannot produce this, and zeroing the count field on a copy yields `integrity_check` = `ok` with all pages accounted for (the freelist is genuinely empty; the count is stale).
- Header bytes 24–27 equal bytes 92–95 on both hosts (change counter == version-valid-for: 0x000D2167 host 1, 0x0003B76A host 2). Per the file-format docs these are stamped equal only by a normally completed commit: the corrupt page 1 was **committed**, not left by an interrupted or rolled-back write.
- Journal mode is `delete` (podman does not set a journal mode; rollback default). On host 2 the entire storage directory was captured with the engine idle: `db.sql` present, no `-journal`/`-wal`/`-shm` sibling; no hot journal.
- Ruled out on both hosts (full syslog/journal review): kernel I/O or ext4 errors, ENOSPC (9% disk used), OOM kills, segfaults, killed podman processes (every cleanup process in the failure window logged normal completion), engine restarts, package activity, manual podman invocations (shell history), and `database is locked` messages (zero, ever). GCE VMs: ECC memory, replicated PD.
- Concurrency at onset was routine: 5 distinct podman pids logged within the failure second, a level matched in thousands of other seconds over the hosts’ lifetimes (max observed 13). No spike.
- The onset is bounded to the final seconds: libpod’s 5-minute ContainerExitCode prune (a multi-row DELETE that frees pages) ran within the onset second, and exit-code insert/prune churn plus container create/remove made freelist traffic near-constant, so a latent bad header would have failed almost immediately. The freelist is the contended structure.

**Hypothesis (labeled as such, not proven):** the damage shape (two writers’ views of the freelist merged into one committed page 1) matches what breaking POSIX advisory locks would allow (howtocorrupt.html section 2.2, locks canceled by `close()`). Noting for completeness: SQLite 3.51.0’s new broken-lock defenses would not help here even if available, since they apply only in WAL mode and podman opens the DB in rollback mode. SQLite 3.45.1 (Ubuntu 24.04) has no detection.

**Why we’re filing now:** a search of this tracker for “database disk image is malformed” on 2026-09-04 returned zero issues, so this failure mode appears unknown upstream, while the 5.8 boltdb-to-sqlite auto-migration and the 6.0 boltdb removal are moving the entire remaining userbase onto this backend. We verified the sqlite connection options are identical in v4.9.3, v5.4.0, and current main (`_sync=FULL`, `_txlock=exclusive`, busy timeout, no journal-mode option, no `database/sql` pool cap), so nothing in newer podman changes the access pattern involved.

**Suggestions we’d like considered:**

1.  Open the state DB in WAL mode: commits stop funneling through page 1 on every transaction, and it enables SQLite ≥3.51.0’s broken-lock defenses on distros that ship it.
2.  Cap the `database/sql` connection pool (or serialize writers) in the API service.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

No minimal reproducer yet. The workload shape that produced it twice:

1.  Rootful podman 4.9.3 API service (socket-activated) on Ubuntu 24.04, sqlite backend, defaults otherwise.
2.  Sustained churn from many concurrent API clients: ~15 containers in flight, ~1.9 create/start/wait/remove cycles per second, for hours. Conmon-spawned `container cleanup` processes and the `podman-auto-update` timer also open the DB.
3.  Corruption struck at 8.2 h on one host and 1.6 h on another; we have not yet run a controlled soak. We’re happy to run an A/B soak (sqlite vs boltdb arms at this churn rate) and report back if that would help.


### Describe the results you received

After hours of clean operation, mid-churn and with no external fault:

    Request Failed(Internal Server Error): removing container 2ee7f86d[...] from database:
    removing container 2ee7f86d[...] config from database: database disk image is malformed

All subsequent state-changing operations fail the same way; `podman info` after reboot fails with `Error: removing container exit codes: database disk image is malformed`. Recovery requires wiping the store.


### Describe the results you expected

The state DB survives sustained concurrent container churn indefinitely, or at minimum fails in a way that identifies the writer at fault.

### podman info output

```yaml
Not obtainable from the corrupted hosts (see failure output above; both were replaced). Versions below; happy to provide `podman info` from an identically provisioned healthy host on request.
```

### Podman in a container

No

### Privileged Or Rootless

Privileged

### Upstream Latest Release

No

### Additional environment details

- GCE VMs (us-central1-f), Ubuntu 24.04 (noble), kernel 6.17.0-1022-gcp
- podman 4.9.3+ds1-1ubuntu0.2, conmon 2.1.10+ds1-1build2, crun 1.14.1-1
- libsqlite3-0 3.45.1-1ubuntu2.7 (dynamically linked; single sqlite copy per `ldd`), mattn/go-sqlite3 v1.14.18
- ext4 on PD; no NFS or shared storage anywhere near the DB

### Additional information

- Two corrupted db.sql files with matching signatures are retained; we can share page-1 hexdumps (offsets 0–100), full `PRAGMA integrity_check` output, and log excerpts on request. We cannot attach the raw DB files (container configs in them include environment values).
- Timeline and log evidence are precise to the millisecond on both hosts if useful: first failure host 1 at 2026-09-04 00:22:30.530 UTC; host 2 at 2026-09-04 11:23:26 UTC.
- Mitigation on our side: pinned `database_backend = "boltdb"` fleet-wide, which is why the boltdb removal timeline matters to us.

title: podman stop: network teardown fails with "netavark: setns: IO error: Invalid argument" on kernel 6.12.0-211.7.3.el10_2; stale socket leaves published port bound but black-holed

body:
### Issue Description

`podman stop` (or systemd/quadlet stop) consistently fails during container network teardown on
kernel 6.12.0-211.7.3.el10_2.x86_64, with journal errors:

    Error: cleaning up container <id>: removing container <id> network: netavark: setns: IO error: Invalid argument (os error 22)
    unit: Control process exited, code=exited, status=125/n/a

Beyond the failed teardown, a stale socket survives on the container's published host port
(owned by conmon), so every TCP connect to that port times out afterwards. Every *fresh*
container created after such a failure has its published port black-holed the same way,
even though the iptables DNAT / nftables jump rules are all present and correct.
A host reboot clears both symptoms until the next failing teardown.

Same machine, same packages, kernel 6.12.0-211.49.1.el10_2.x86_64: zero failures across
dozens of start/stop cycles. Only difference between failing and clean runs is the kernel.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. AlmaLinux 10.2 host (bare-metal or VM), podman 5.8.2 / crun 1.27 / netavark 1.17.2, systemd 257, kernel 6.12.0-211.7.3.el10_2.x86_64
2. podman network create mynet (or systemctl start of any quadlet container unit with a published TCP port)
3. podman stop <container>   -> journal shows the EINVAL netavark/setns error above, exit status 125
4. systemctl/podman start the container again; curl its published port from localhost -> connect times out
5. podman exec/ss: socket still LISTEN on the published port, fd owned by conmon; any other new container's published port behaves identically

### Describe the results you received

- stop always fails at teardown with "netavark: setns: IO error: Invalid argument (os error 22)" (100% repro on the .7.3 kernel)
- published host port remains LISTEN (socket owner conmon fd5) but all connects to it time out
- subsequently created containers have their published ports dead in the same way despite valid DNAT rules
- firewalld ruleset verified correct (accept rules present) - firewall ruled out
- only cleared by a host reboot; recurs after further stops

### Describe the results you expected

stop succeeds (network teardown completes), unit reaches inactive cleanly, and the published port
serves the restarted (and any new) container on the same kernel that hosts containers without issue
(6.12.0-211.49.1.el10_2.x86_64 - dozens of stop/start cycles clean).

  clean:   6.12.0-211.49.1.el10_2.x86_64 (dnf install of the current el10_2 kernel)
systemd 257-23.el10_2.2.alma.1, SELinux enforcing, iptables frontend, default netavark network setup.
Repro box: pristine libvirt VM (fresh Alma 10.2), stock busybox httpd container, no custom CNI/firewall -
same signature also occurred on the original bare-metal host (Rocky 9, podman 5.9.4).

- Frequency: 100% of stops fail on .7.3 (journal shows every single teardown error); dozens of stop/start cycles clean on 49.1 on the same box/packages

- Since only the kernel changes between failing and clean runs, the EINVAL from setns() at teardown time (and the leftover socket state) may be kernel-side - feel free to point it to the right project/kernel bug tracker

**PR Description:**
- Problem: Container prune documentation claims that podman container prune removes all stopped containers from local storage. However, stopped containers that belong to pods are not removed. This behavior was confirmed by the reporter in #29213.
- Investigation: Runtime.PruneContainers() filters out all containers that have a Pod ID before checking their status.([`libpod/runtime_ctr.go:1350-1356`](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/blob/main/libpod/runtime_ctr.go#L1350-L1356)) As a result, stopped containers that belong to pods never reach the size calculation or removal logic.

title: rootless: RunUnderSystemdScope waits forever on the StartTransientUnit job channel when the systemd manager never completes the job
body:
### What happened?

Every rootless podman command can hang **forever, with no output and no error**, when the systemd manager never completes the transient-unit job that `RunUnderSystemdScope` waits for.

`RunUnderSystemdScope` ends with:

```go
	ch := make(chan string)
	_, err = conn.StartTransientUnitContext(context.Background(), unitName, "replace", properties, ch)
	if err != nil { ... }

	// Block until job is started
	<-ch

	return nil
```

The `<-ch` read has **no timeout and does not honor the context**. For rootless callers the connection goes to the *user* manager (`cgroups.UserConnection`); if that manager accepts the `StartTransientUnit` call but the job is never removed (wedged user manager, job queued behind a never-completing job, a lost `JobRemoved` signal), the read blocks for eternity. The scope move is best-effort cgroup hygiene on the startup path of **every** rootless podman command (`SetupRootless` → `MovePauseProcessToScope`, and the `euid == 0` branch for the re-exec'd process), so a wedged manager turns into "every rootless podman invocation silently hangs until killed" — and because failures in this helper are only logged at debug level, there is no diagnostic output at all.

This is not hypothetical: on GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runners, a rootless `podman info` probe run as a non-login system user (uid 999, linger enabled, cgroup v2 delegation healthy) hung until killed (exit 124) on 11 consecutive CI dispatches, reproducible on every attempt within one runner instance. The podman debug log always ends at

```
time="..." level=info msg="Setting parallel job count to 7"
```

which is printed immediately *before* `SetupRootless` reaches the scope-move path — nothing further is ever printed. (For completeness: in our case the stall finally turned out to be compounded by a separate problem — a lock region left by a different podman version shadowing the distro binary; but the unbounded systemd wait below is real and was separately reproduced.)

A minimal demonstration of the failure class: run any rootless podman command with the user's systemd manager unresponsive (`kill -STOP $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value user@$(id -u).service)`), and the command hangs until externally killed. Pointing `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` / `DBUS_SYSTEM_BUS_ADDRESS` at a dead socket so the connection fails fast makes the hang unreachable — which is how we currently work around it in CI, and rootless containers (pull, build, `podman run --network pasta`) keep working with the scope move degraded, so treating this call as truly best-effort is safe.

### Expected behavior

The wait for the job should be bounded and cancellable — e.g. `select` on the channel, `ctx.Done()` and a timeout — degrading to a debug-logged failure like the other error paths of this helper, instead of wedging the whole command.

### Environment

- Present in podman 5.8.4 via `go.podman.io/common` (`pkg/systemd/systemd_linux.go:104-152` in the vendored module)
- Present in podman 4.9.x (`utils/utils_supported.go:59-60`) — the version shipped in Ubuntu 24.04, where we hit it
- Ubuntu 24.04, cgroup v2, systemd 255, rootless

title: Podman should not obsess over using systemd by default on systemd systems.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

body:
### Feature request description

I recently decided to switch from Docker to Podman as I find the daemonless approach very enticing.
I am running Podman on Debian 13, which uses systemd by default.
With the recent controversy regarding systemd (which is **not** the point of this request), I am considering moving from systemd to another boot manager.
When using Podman, even when telling Podman to use cgroupsf, it keeps obsessing about systemd regularly.
For example, running a simple Stalwart container will produce the following error:
```
ERRO[0000] failed to move the rootless netns pasta process to the systemd user.slice: dial unix /run/user/0/bus: connect: permission denied 
```
I understand this error, but Podman is a container runner, it should not obsess over using a boot manager as orchestrator by default.

### Suggest potential solution

Podman should avoid trying to obsessively rely on systemd when installed on a systemd system.
It should be an opt-in instead of an opt-out. If it has to stay opt-out, then the opt-out should not require such a painful process of untangling every single configuration out of systemd.

### Have you considered any alternatives?

I understand why some people would want to use systemd. I think it is also understandable why other people would not want to use systemd.

### Additional context

A few reasons why I do not want to use systemd aside from the controversy:
- systemd is not a container orchestrator, it's not designed for this, it's not its responsibility.
- managing all container logs through journald is not something I am interested in. It would require a considerable machinery and a lot of engineering for something that is already trivially solved using a normal container orchestration.
- I do not want any non administrator manipulating systemctl.

title: completion: also claim the .exe name in generated scripts
body:
## Summary

On Windows the binary is `podman.exe`, so in Git Bash typing `podman` and
pressing TAB completes the *command word* to `podman.exe` before argument
completion runs. Bash looks up completion specs by the exact command word,
and the script from `podman completion bash` registers only one name:

    complete -o default -F __start_podman podman

There is no spec for `podman.exe`, so bash falls back to file name
completion. The completion logic is fine — it is never reached, because the
name it is registered under is not the name being typed. The work-around in
the issue, `sed 's/podman$/podman podman.exe/'`, is exactly the missing
registration.

## Related Issue

Fixes: #29685

## Changes

**bash:** cobra emits the `complete` line from `c.Name()` and only ever emits
one. `completion()` already appends to cobra's output — the trailing
`# This file is generated with "podman completion"` comment is ours — so the
second registration goes through the same `io.WriteString`. It points at
`__start_podman`, the function cobra already generated, so no logic is
duplicated, only a second name bound to it. The `compopt` check mirrors
cobra's own, keeping the `-o nospace` fallback for bash 3.

The name comes from `cmd.Root().Name()` rather than a literal, so
`podman-remote` gets `podman-remote.exe` from the same code path. `root.go`
already builds it as `strings.TrimSuffix(filepath.Base(os.Args[0]), ".exe")`,
so `podman.exe completion bash` cannot produce `podman.exe.exe`.

**powershell:** a second `Register-ArgumentCompleter` reusing the same
completer block, with cobra's `-` to `_` sanitization for the variable name —
otherwise the podman-remote script would reference
`${__podman-remoteCompleterBlock}`, which is never declared.

Plus the regenerated `completions/` files.

## Steps to Test

The test fails without the fix:

    PODMAN=$(pwd)/bin/podman bats -f "claim the .exe" test/system/600-completion.bats

It asserts both generated scripts register the `.exe` name, deriving the
expected name from `$PODMAN` so it covers `podman-remote` too.

That the committed files match the generator:

    make completions && git diff --exit-code completions/

Directly: `source <(./bin/podman completion bash)`, then `complete -p
podman.exe` — no completion specification before, `-F __start_podman
podman.exe` after. On Windows, in Git Bash, `podman` TAB (completing to
`podman.exe`) then TAB again now gives subcommands instead of file names.

## Notes for the Reviewer

@Luap99 you noted these scripts come from cobra, not from us, and that is
right — the template cannot be fixed here. This changes only what podman
appends after cobra is done, which `completion()` already does.

I think there is a case for podman carrying it rather than waiting on
upstream: we ship a Windows binary, it is called `podman.exe`, and
podman-completion(1) already tells Windows users to invoke it that way. The
cobra fix helps every cobra CLI and is worth doing, but needs a release and a
vendor bump before a Windows user sees anything. Happy to open that PR
instead, or as well — say which you prefer.

zsh and fish are untouched, since neither is the shell this happens in.

title: podman build --secret leaves secrets in plaintext next to the build context

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: macos
labels.description: MacOS (OSX) related

body:
### Issue Description

A successful `podman build --secret` leaves a plaintext copy of the secret on the host and does not remove it. The copy lands in the parent directory of the build context, mode 0600. Not in `TMPDIR` or somewhere else.

This looks like a leftover from #28356, which fixed #25314 and #28334 by moving these temp files under the primary context. Both of those were about the secret ending up inside the image, or the build failing. This is the opposite direction: the build succeeds, the image is clean, and the secret stays on the host.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

No compose, no registry, no `.dockerignore`. Build from a third directory:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/fixture/ctx /tmp/fixture/elsewhere
echo "s3cr3t-value" > /tmp/fixture/mysecret
printf 'FROM docker.io/library/alpine:3.20\nRUN --mount=type=secret,id=tok cat /run/secrets/tok\n' \
  > /tmp/fixture/ctx/Dockerfile

cd /tmp/fixture/elsewhere
podman build --secret id=tok,src=/tmp/fixture/mysecret -t leaktest /tmp/fixture/ctx
ls -l /tmp/fixture
```

### Describe the results you received

The build succeeds, with no error and no warning:
```
STEP 2/2: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=tok cat /run/secrets/tok
s3cr3t-value
COMMIT leaktest
--> 5731f2f459f9
Successfully tagged localhost/leaktest:latest
```

The secret is then sitting in the context's parent:
```bash
$ find /tmp/fixture | sort
/tmp/fixture
/tmp/fixture/ctx
/tmp/fixture/ctx/Dockerfile
/tmp/fixture/elsewhere
/tmp/fixture/mysecret
/tmp/fixture/podman-build-secret-1695017466      <- left behind

$ ls -l /tmp/fixture/podman-build-secret-1695017466
-rw-------  1 me  wheel  13 Aug 31 16:17 /tmp/fixture/podman-build-secret-1695017466

$ cat /tmp/fixture/podman-build-secret-1695017466
s3cr3t-value                                      <- the secret, in plaintext
```

Two things about the location:
- Not the working directory. The build ran from `/tmp/fixture/elsewhere`, which stayed empty.
- Not the context. `/tmp/fixture/ctx` still holds only the Dockerfile.

The second one surprised me, because the code passes the context directory. In v6.1.0, `prepareSecrets` does:
```go
tmpSecret, err := tempManager.CreateTempFileFromReader(contextDir, "podman-build-secret-*", ...)
```
and `CreateTempFileFromReader` is a plain `os.CreateTemp(dest, pattern)`. So I would expect the file in the context, not one level above it.

### Describe the results you expected

The file is removed when the build finishes. That already looks like the intent: `build()` has `defer tempManager.Cleanup()`, `CreateTempFileFromReader` registers the file with `AddFile` before writing to it, and `Cleanup()` calls `os.Remove` on everything registered.

`Cleanup()` also logs `Failed to remove temp file %s: %v` on any error other than "already gone", and there is no such line in the output. So cleanup is not failing loudly. It is not reaching this file at all.

### podman info output

```yaml
Client:
  APIVersion: 6.1.0
  BuildOrigin: brew
  Built: 1786554266
  BuiltTime: Wed Aug 12 19:04:26 2026
  GoVersion: go1.26.5
  Os: darwin
  OsArch: darwin/arm64
  Version: 6.1.0
host:
  arch: arm64
  buildahVersion: 1.44.0
  cgroupManager: systemd
  cgroupVersion: v2
  cpus: 10
  databaseBackend: sqlite
  distribution:
    distribution: fedora
    variant: podman-machine-os
    version: "44"
```

### Podman in a container

No

### Privileged Or Rootless

Rootless

### Upstream Latest Release

Yes

### Additional environment details

```bash
$ podman version
Client:  Version: 6.1.0   Build Origin: brew   OS/Arch: darwin/arm64
Server:  Version: 6.1.0   OS/Arch: linux/arm64

$ podman machine ssh rpm -q podman
podman-6.1.0-1.20260812170728687735.pr29481.11.cade97a52e.fc44.aarch64

$ podman machine ssh sudo bootc status | grep image:
    image: quay.io/podman/machine-os:6.1

$ sw_vers
ProductName:     macOS
ProductVersion:  26.6.2
BuildVersion:    25G83

$ system_profiler SPHardwareDataType
Model Name:       MacBook Pro
Model Identifier: Mac16,7
Chip:             Apple M4 Pro
...
```
applehv, rootless. Nothing configured on my side: no `containers.conf` and no `storage.conf` at either `~/.config/containers/` or `/etc/containers/`. The repro has no `.dockerignore` at all, so #25314 seems like a different issue.

### Additional information

Impact, in case it is not obvious from something that looks like a stray temp file: this is a credential written to a directory the user did not choose and is not watching. In my case it was a short-lived Google Artifact Registry token, so a handful accumulated next to my repo checkouts before I noticed, which is survivable. A long-lived secret would not be. A build context at the root of a synced folder would not be either.

title: Use Windows GUI version of gvproxy on arm64 too
body:
`gvproxy` is released in two flavors on Windows: GUI and Console. The GUI version is what we want: it doesn't inherit the parent process console and isn't killed if the parent console is closed.

On amd64 we already pulled the GUI version but not for the arm64 version (the names on the gvisor-tap-vsock release page don't help). This commit fixes this problem.

Related to https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/issues/29573

podman bash completion should claim `podman` and `podman.exe`.
If you use Podman from Git Bash on Windows, the command might complete to `podman.exe` and then the completion done by `source <(podman completion bash)` does not trigger.

title: libpod: fix :O overlay volumes in a userns
body:
When the user owning the storage is not mapped into the container user namespace (e.g. root with --userns=auto), the runtime cannot mount an overlay volume from inside the user namespace.

Mount the overlay in podman instead and pass the runtime a bind mount.

Closes: https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/issues/28758

title: hack/ci: list ginkgo failures in the summary
body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Follow-up to the thing I mentioned in #29682. The tail summary you added in 66c6da6 only ever lists bats failures - `__fail_list` is pushed to inside the bats branch and nowhere else - so for the e2e suites the part of the log github actually shows says nothing about what broke.

Before, on the ginkgo sample that is already in `logformatter.t`:

```
Ran 1889 of 2014 Specs in 1607.919 seconds
FAIL! -- 1881 Passed | 1 Failed | 0 Pending | 125 Skipped
```

after:

```
Ran 1889 of 2014 Specs in 1607.919 seconds
FAIL! -- 1881 Passed | 1 Failed | 0 Pending | 125 Skipped

Failed tests (1):
 - Podman pod create podman pod correctly sets up PIDNS
```

It hooks the `[FAIL] ... [It] ...` line that is already parsed for the anchor link, so the name is the same one the html links to. bats output is unchanged, and a run with no failures still prints nothing.

#### How to verify it

First commit is on its own because the harness sent stdout to `/dev/null`, so nothing covered the tail summary at all, not even the existing bats one. It adds a `%%%` section for expected stdout. The second commit's test fails without the change:

```
not ok 4 - simple ginkgo (stdout)
#     $got->[0] = Does not exist
#     $expected->[0] = 'Failed tests (1):'
```

#### One thing I got wrong on the way

My first attempt pushed onto `$bats_count`, which made `keys %bats_count` true for ginkgo runs and printed an empty `Summary:. Total tests: 0` line into the html. The existing test caught it, hence the separate list.

title: hack/ci: fix apiv2 test count warning
body: #### What this PR does / why we need it: I was reading logformatter after the aarch64 timeout on #29569, where a run stopped part way through and I wanted to know how the "expected N" warning decides. It turns out apiv2 trips it on every run. `/test-apiv2` in the command line sets `expected_total = -1` as a "we do not know the count yet" marker, and the plan line then does `+=` on it, so the sentinel is added instead of replaced. test-apiv2 prints `1..${test_count}` at the very end, so it always lands one short: ``` Summary: 3 Passed. Total tests: 3 (WARNING: expected 2) ``` That run was complete. With the fix: ``` Summary: 3 Passed. Total tests: 3 ``` and a run that really did stop early still warns: ``` Total tests: 2 (WARNING: expected 815) ``` #### How to verify it Added a case to `logformatter.t`, it fails on current main: ``` not ok 5 - bats plan line at end of run # $got->[4] = '... Total tests: 2 (WARNING: expected 1)...' # $expected->[4] = '... Total tests: 2' ``` #### One thing I noticed but did not touch The mismatch warning is only written into the HTML, and the tail summary you added in 66c6da6 does not mention it. So a run that stops early looks clean in the GitHub log, which is the case I hit on #29569. cc @Luap99

title: lint: catch unchecked index after strings.Split
body:
Two recent fixes were the same bug in different places: `strings.Split` on a two-field parse, where the delimiter can also occur inside the value.

- #29653, remote `ImageEngine.Prune` split `--filter` on every `=`, so the documented `label=version=1.0` matched nothing
- #29654, `subpath=` kept only the text between the first and second `=`, so a path containing `=` mounted a different directory

I audited the tree for the pattern: 160 `strings.Split*` sites outside vendor and tests, and 137 already use `SplitN` or check `len()` before indexing. The convention exists, it just is not enforced.

`.golangci.yml` already forbids `os.Is*` through forbidigo, with the reason in a comment: those functions "subtly fail to deal with other wrapped error types". An unchecked index after `Split` has the same shape. forbidigo cannot express it, since banning `strings.Split` would flag the 137 correct uses, but `gocritic` is enabled and ruleguard can match `strings.Split($s, $sep)[$i]` without a preceding length check.

Would you take a ruleguard rule for this? Happy to write it and the exclusions.

title: use systemd unit name for healthcheck units
body:
# Description

Fixes: #29373 

The issue asks for healthcheck units to use a consistent name instead of using the container ID with a random suffix.

This change uses the libpod-healthcheck- prefix with the container ID to create the healthcheck unit name.

For example:

`libpod-healthcheck-<container-id>-<rand-hex>.service`
`libpod-healthcheck-<container-id>-<rand-hex>.timer`

The container ID and random suffix are kept to make the healthcheck unit names unique.

Added unit tests to verify the healthcheck unit name, startup healthcheck name, and bare behavior.

title: generate/kube API endpoint sends Content-Type: application/x-tar instead of text/vnd.yaml

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

body:
### Issue Description

The `GET /libpod/generate/kube` endpoint (used by `podman generate kube` / `podman kube
generate`, and callable directly via the libpod HTTP API) returns Kubernetes YAML but
labels it with the wrong `Content-Type`: `application/x-tar` instead of `text/vnd.yaml`.

This contradicts the endpoint's own swagger docs in pkg/api/server/register_kube.go:

    // produces:
    // - text/vnd.yaml
    // - application/json

Root cause: the handler (pkg/api/handlers/libpod/generate.go) sends the YAML through the
shared utils.WriteResponse() helper, whose io.Reader branch hardcodes
`application/x-tar` it was built for the tar-streaming endpoints (image save/export,
`podman cp`) that are its other callers, and GenerateKube just reuses that path.

There's already a FIXME in generate.go calling this out, unresolved:

    // FIXME: Content-Type is being set as application/x-tar NOT text/vnd.yaml

Any client that trusts the documented Content-Type to parse the response (e.g. an SDK
generated from the swagger spec) will treat plain YAML text as a tar archive.

I've root-caused this and have a small patch ready  a WriteResponseWithContentType
helper alongside WriteResponse, so the other tar-streaming callers are untouched. 

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Start the podman API service:
   podman system service --time=0 unix:///tmp/podman.sock &
2. Create any container, e.g.:
   podman run -d --name test-gen alpine sleep 300
3. Query the generate/kube endpoint directly and inspect the response headers:
   curl -i --unix-socket /tmp/podman.sock "http://d/v5.0.0/libpod/generate/kube?names=test-gen"

### Describe the results you received

HTTP response headers include:
  Content-Type: application/x-tar

...while the response body is plain Kubernetes YAML text not
a tar archive.

### Describe the results you expected

Content-Type: text/vnd.yaml (or another appropriate text/YAML media type), matching the
"produces: text/vnd.yaml" declared in this endpoint's own swagger documentation in
pkg/api/server/register_kube.go.

### podman info output

```yaml
main branch,
version 6.2.0-dev, commit 7a6c0a0 (2026-08-28)

Podman version: 6.2.0-dev (main branch, commit 7a6c0a0, 2026-08-28)

unable to run verified this via source code
```

title: pkg/bindings, pkg/api: send the manifest index subject to the server

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Change to remote API; merits scrutiny

body:
podman manifest annotate --index --subject and podman manifest add --artifact-subject both work locally but do nothing when you run them with --remote. The flags are there and the commands exit fine, the subject just never gets set.

The value never leaves the client. The bindings copy everything into ModifyOptions and AddArtifactOptions before sending the request and neither struct had a field for the subject, so it was dropped. The server had a problem of its own too… ManifestModify rebuilds ManifestAddArtifactOptions by hand and left out the embedded ManifestAnnotateOptions, so --os, --arch and --annotation were getting dropped there as well.

This adds the field to both structs with the json name the server expects, regenerates the setters with go generate, forwards the value from the tunnel, and passes the annotate options along in the handler. I dropped the bindings unit test and added two system tests in test/system/012-manifest.bats instead, one per flag, and neither is skipped on remote.

title: pkg/domain/infra/tunnel: error when signing a remote push
body:
I noticed that podman push --sign-by works fine locally but does nothing when
you run it with --remote. The remote client never sends the signing options
across, so the push finishes, tells you it worked, and you are left with an
unsigned image and no warning.

I have not tried to make remote signing work here, that is a much bigger job.
This just makes push, manifest push and artifact push fail with a clear error
instead of quietly pretending. The check goes right next to the ones that were
already there for Signers and encryption and says much the same thing. artifact
push did not have any check at all so it gets both.

title: Compat API: attach to an exited container resets its state and destroys the recorded exit code
body:
### Issue Description

Attaching to an **already-exited** container through the Docker-compatible HTTP API resets that container's state and destroys its recorded exit code. The container reverts from `exited` to `created`, `State.ExitCode` is reset to `0`, and a subsequent `POST /containers/{id}/wait` returns `{"StatusCode":-1}`.

The real exit code is not recoverable afterwards — the engine no longer holds it.

This is a read operation from the caller's point of view, so the data loss is silent and unexpected: the response itself is a normal `200` with the expected log frames, and nothing signals that anything was destroyed.

Notably, `podman attach` on the CLI refuses this case (`can only attach to created or running containers`, cf. #9597, #23757), but the compat API endpoint does not.

`GET /containers/{id}/logs` on the same container does **not** have this effect, and Docker does not have it at all.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

```bash
SOCK=/run/user/1000/podman/podman.sock
N=attach-exitcode-probe

curl -s -o /dev/null -XPOST --unix-socket $SOCK -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"Image":"alpine","Cmd":["sh","-c","exit 4"]}' \
  "http://d/v1.41/containers/create?name=$N"
curl -s -o /dev/null -XPOST --unix-socket $SOCK "http://d/v1.41/containers/$N/start"
curl -s -o /dev/null -XPOST --unix-socket $SOCK "http://d/v1.41/containers/$N/wait"

echo -n 'before: '; curl -s --unix-socket $SOCK "http://d/v1.41/containers/$N/json" \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin)["State"]; print(d["Status"], d["ExitCode"])'
echo -n 'wait:   '; curl -s -XPOST --unix-socket $SOCK "http://d/v1.41/containers/$N/wait"

# the attach that does it -- stream=0, so it returns immediately
curl -s -o /dev/null -XPOST --unix-socket $SOCK \
  "http://d/v1.41/containers/$N/attach?stream=0&logs=1&stdout=1&stderr=1"

echo -n 'after:  '; curl -s --unix-socket $SOCK "http://d/v1.41/containers/$N/json" \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin)["State"]; print(d["Status"], d["ExitCode"])'
echo -n 'wait:   '; curl -s -XPOST --unix-socket $SOCK "http://d/v1.41/containers/$N/wait"
```

### Describe the results you received

```
before: exited 4
wait:   {"StatusCode":4,"Error":null}
after:  created 0
wait:   {"StatusCode":-1,"Error":null}
```

All three attach variants trigger it — `stream=1&logs=1`, `stream=1` alone, and the `stream=0&logs=1` shown above, which returns cleanly in a couple of milliseconds. It is the call itself, not the hang that `stream=1` produces against an exited container.

### Describe the results you expected

Attaching to an exited container should either be refused (as the CLI does) or be a no-op with respect to container state. The recorded exit code should survive, so that:

```
after:  exited 4
wait:   {"StatusCode":4}
```

Docker behaves this way — same probe against Docker 29.7.2 (API 1.55) leaves `exited 4` and `wait` `{"StatusCode":4}` untouched.

### podman info output

```yaml
version:
  APIVersion: 5.8.4
  Version: 5.8.4
  OsArch: linux/amd64
host:
  os: linux
  kernel: 6.12.94+deb13-amd64
  distribution: Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie)
  rootless: true
  conmon: 2.1.12
  ociRuntime: crun
```

Reproduced identically on **5.8.4** and on **5.4.2** (the version Debian 13 ships), rootless in both cases.

### Podman in a container

No

### Privileged Or Rootless

Rootless

### Upstream Latest Release

Yes

### Additional environment details

Found while building a pure-Perl Docker Engine API client that is tested against both Podman and Docker. The client now has to ask `inspect` whether the container is running and refuse the attach itself, which costs a round trip and still leaves a race — the container can stop between the check and the attach, and the exit code is then lost the same way. There is no attach-if-running option in the API, so this cannot be fully solved on the client side.

title: machine: ensure OCI pull cache directory exists
body:
## What does this PR do?

Fixes `podman machine init` failing on Windows with:

```text
The system cannot find the path specified.
```

when the OCI machine image cache parent directory does not exist.

## Why?

`pkg/machine/ocipull/pull.go` passes the destination path to `layout.ParseReference()`. On Windows, the path resolution performed by `containers/image` requires the parent directory to exist.

When the cache parent directory is missing, this results in `ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND`.

This change creates the destination's parent directory with `os.MkdirAll()` before calling `layout.ParseReference()`.

The final OCI layout directory is not created beforehand. It is still created by `containers/image` during the pull.

## Testing

Added a regression test covering the missing parent directory case.

The following targeted test passes:

```text
go test -tags containers_image_openpgp ./pkg/machine/ocipull -run TestPullCreatesParentDirectory -v
```

The complete `pkg/machine/ocipull` package test suite also passes.

Fixes #29639

title: rootless: read all of /proc/<pid>/environ when checking for a pause process
body:
Fixes #29650.

#29657 is already open against the same issue and comes at it from the other end:
it calls `clearenv()` before `setenv("_PODMAN_PAUSE", "1", 1)`, so the pause
process carries almost nothing and the marker lands inside the first chunk. That
does stop the bug I hit, and its second hunk — null-terminating the buffer — is
the out-of-bounds walk I flagged in the issue. I'm not putting this up instead of
that one; it fixes a different half, and I'm happy with whichever shape you prefer,
including folding the two together.

What made me write this is that `clearenv()` changes what goes *into* the pause
process rather than what `is_pause_process()` is willing to *read*, and two things
live through that:

**Pause processes that already exist.** Upgrading podman doesn't restart the pause
process. Anyone who updates while holding one created by an older build still has a
large environment on the other end, so the first command after the upgrade can
still unlink a valid `pause.pid` and leave every running container unreachable.
That is a bad moment for it to happen, because it reads as the upgrade having
broken the containers.

**The asymmetry with the Go side.** `isPauseProcess()` in `rootless_linux.go` uses
`os.ReadFile` and reads the whole file. The C twin reading a single chunk is the
odd one out, and it stays odd: a later change that puts anything else in the pause
process's environment brings this back silently, with the same consequence.

So this reads to EOF, which is what the Go implementation already does. The buffer
grows with an explicit 16 MB ceiling so a misbehaving procfs can't make it grow
without bound, and each comparison is bounded by the number of bytes actually read,
since `read()` can stop mid-entry and `strcmp`/`strlen` would then run past the end
of the buffer.

### Testing

I lifted `is_pause_process()` into a standalone harness, once from `main` and once
from this branch, and ran both against two processes that differ only in how much
padding they carry:

```
$ env -i PAD=short _PODMAN_PAUSE=1 sleep 60 & SMALL=$!
$ env -i PAD=$(printf 'x%.0s' $(seq 1 4200)) _PODMAN_PAUSE=1 sleep 60 & BIG=$!

proces                       old          new
environ=26     B (SMALL)     1            1
environ=4221   B (BIG)       0            1
```

The 26-byte row is there to show the case that already worked still works.

Both files compile clean under `gcc -Wall -Wextra`.

title: rootless: clear environment before spawning pause process

labels.name: No New Tests
labels.description: Allow PR to proceed without adding regression tests

body:
<!-- Please include a concise description of your changes -->
### Description
When spawning the pause process in `pkg/rootless/rootless_linux.c`, the process inherited environment variables from the parent process before setting `_PODMAN_PAUSE=1`. If the parent environment exceeded 4096 bytes (the chunk size read by `is_pause_process`), `_PODMAN_PAUSE=1` was placed beyond the first 4KB chunk, causing `is_pause_process` to treat a healthy pause process as stale and unlink its `pause.pid` file.

This PR calls `clearenv()` before setting `_PODMAN_PAUSE=1` so the pause process only carries the necessary marker at index 0. Additionally, `is_pause_process()` safely null-terminates its read buffer.

Fixes: #29650
Signed-off-by: sundeep8967 <sundeep8967@gmail.com>

title: api: reflect container stats errors in HTTP status codes

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Change to remote API; merits scrutiny

body:
Existing `KillContainer` handling uses HTTP status code 409 when the request cannot be performed because of the current container state. HTTP status code 404 is also used when the target container does not exist.

In contrast, errors from the stats handler are not reflected in the HTTP status code. The HTTP status code is always 200, and the errors are recorded only as generic errors in the server log.

To maintain compatibility with both streaming enabled and disabled, this change treats obtaining at least one complete unit of response content as the response contract. It then keeps the response content consistent with the HTTP status code.

title: fix(libpod): keep '=' in a volume subpath
body:
The subpath mount option is parsed with `strings.Split(o, "=")[1]`, so it keeps only the text between the first and second `=`. A subpath that contains `=` gets cut short and the container mounts a different directory than the one that was asked for.

```
--mount type=volume,src=v,dst=/mnt,subpath=/opt/a=b/c   mounts /opt/a
```

The existing subpath e2e test now uses a path with an `=` in it.

title: fix(remote): keep '=' in a prune filter value
body:
`ImageEngine.Prune` on the remote path splits each `--filter` on every `=` and keeps
everything after the first as separate values, so a filter whose value itself contains
`=` gets torn apart.

`podman-image-prune.1.md` documents `label=key=value` and gives `--filter label=version=1.0`
as an example. Today that produces

    filters["label"] = ["version", "1.0"]

instead of `["version=1.0"]`. libimage turns every element into its own label filter and
`MatchLabelFilters` cuts each one on `=` itself, so the request becomes "has a label key
`version`" AND "has a label key `1.0`". Nothing carries a key named `1.0`, so the prune
matches no images and silently removes nothing.

Local podman is unaffected: the abi path passes `opts.Filter` through untouched. This is
remote-only, and it diverges from both siblings in the same file. `List` uses
`SplitN(filter, "=", 2)`; `Events` validates then rejoins with `strings.Join`. This change
makes `Prune` mirror `List` exactly.

The existing e2e case only used `label=abc`, a bare key, which survives the old split by
accident. Added one that uses a `key=value` label and checks the non-matching image is
still there afterwards.

Signed-off-by: Atishyy27 <sethatishayjain@gmail.com>

title: is_pause_process() reads only the first 4096 bytes of /proc/<pid>/environ, so a live pause process is treated as stale
body:
Since #28323, when podman fails to join the namespaces named by `pause.pid`, it
decides whether that PID is really a pause process by looking for
`_PODMAN_PAUSE=1` in `/proc/<pid>/environ`, and deletes `pause.pid` when it
doesn't find it. That lookup reads a single 4096-byte chunk. But
`_PODMAN_PAUSE` is added with `setenv()` just before the pause process is
forked (`rootless_linux.c:1102`), so it sits at the *end* of the environment
block — which means any session with more than 4 KB of environment fails the
check, and a perfectly healthy pause process has its pid file removed.

The comment above the read says the entry is searched for in chunks, but there
is only one `read()` (`pkg/rootless/rootless_linux.c:645`, main at `fb1cb4fa6ea4`):

```c
  const size_t buf_size = 4096;
  ...
  /* Read in chunks and search for the null-delimited key=value entry.  */
  n = TEMP_FAILURE_RETRY (read (fd, buf, buf_size));
  if (n <= 0)
    return 0;
```

The Go twin of the same predicate doesn't have this problem —
`isPauseProcess()` in `rootless_linux.go` uses `os.ReadFile` and reads the
whole thing. Only the C constructor path is affected.

### Reproducing it

The function is self-contained, so this needs neither podman nor root. Copy
`is_pause_process()` verbatim out of `rootless_linux.c` into a file, add
`#include <errno.h>` for `TEMP_FAILURE_RETRY`, drop the `cleanup_*` attributes,
and add a `main()` that takes a PID in `argv[1]` and prints three things: the
size of that process's environ, whether it contains `_PODMAN_PAUSE=1`, and what
`is_pause_process()` answers. Then start two processes that differ only in how
much padding they carry:

```console
$ env -i PAD=short _PODMAN_PAUSE=1 sleep 120 & SMALL=$!
$ env -i PAD=$(printf 'x%.0s' $(seq 1 4200)) _PODMAN_PAUSE=1 sleep 120 & BIG=$!
```

```console
$ ./pause-check $SMALL
environ = 26 B, contains _PODMAN_PAUSE=1: yes
is_pause_process(1363760) = 1

$ ./pause-check $BIG
environ = 4221 B, contains _PODMAN_PAUSE=1: yes
is_pause_process(1363761) = 0
```

Both carry the entry; only the size of the environment differs. It is
deterministic and single-threaded — no race involved.

Against the real pause processes on this machine, same result:

```console
$ ./pause-check 1176175
environ = 4515 B, contains _PODMAN_PAUSE=1: yes
is_pause_process(1176175) = 0

$ ./pause-check 2693103
environ = 4377 B, contains _PODMAN_PAUSE=1: yes
is_pause_process(2693103) = 0
```

Those two were created by podman 5.8.4, which predates #28323 and so never runs
the check — but `setenv ("_PODMAN_PAUSE", "1", 1)` is byte-identical there
(`v5.8.4:770` and `main:1102`), so the environment layout a 6.x pause process
gets is the same one shown above.

### What I haven't verified

I have not watched podman 6 actually delete a valid `pause.pid`. This machine
runs 5.8.4, which doesn't carry the code, and I didn't want to reproduce the
consequence on a live system. What is demonstrated above is that the predicate
returns the wrong answer for genuine pause processes; the `unlink()` follows
from it directly at the three call sites in the constructor
(`rootless_linux.c:891`, `:897`, `:903`).

### How much this matters

Less than it first looks, and worth being precise about: the check only runs
*after* `open_namespace()` or `setns()` has already failed, so it never fires on
a healthy path. What it changes is the outcome of a failure that would otherwise
be transient. Instead of that one command failing, `pause.pid` is deleted, and
the next podman command builds a second pause process — a sibling user
namespace, not an ancestor. Containers still running in the first one become
unmanageable: `podman ps` goes on reporting them `Up`, while `exec`, `stop` and
`kill` fail with messages that point at the wrong layer entirely
(`unable to find user root: no matching entries in passwd file`,
`crun: kill: Operation not permitted`, `Error: operation not permitted`).

I have been in exactly that state, though not through this bug — it happened on
5.8.4 for a reason I never managed to establish, so I'm not claiming a causal
link, and that is not what I'm reporting here. I mention it only because of how
long it took to understand: four containers running for a day and a half, all
listed as `Up`, none of them reachable, and nothing anywhere suggesting
`podman system migrate`, which is the way out.

It will also look intermittent, because whether it bites depends on the
environment size of whichever process first brought the pause process up. On
this desktop the numbers sit right on the boundary — plasmashell 2809 B, an
interactive shell 3946 B, the two pause processes 4515 B and 4377 B.

### Suggested direction

The small fix is to read the whole file rather than one chunk, which also makes
the C side agree with the Go side that already does this.

The alternative is to stop asking `environ` in the first place — the question
being answered is "is this the process I think it is", and a check that doesn't
depend on how big someone's environment happens to be would be sturdier. That's
a design call rather than a bug fix, so I've only mentioned it.

### Related hardening, not the defect above

Whatever the buffer ends up being, the scan can walk past what was actually
read. `read()` may stop mid-entry, leaving the tail of `buf` with no NUL in it;
`strcmp (p, ...)` and `strlen (p)` then run past `buf + n`, and when
`n == buf_size` past the end of the allocation. Bounding the scan by `n` seems
worth doing regardless of how the size question is settled.

### Environment

- podman 5.8.4 (`podman-5.8.4-1.fc44.x86_64`, Fedora RPM), rootless, cgroups v2,
  crun 1.28, catatonit 0.2.1
- Fedora 44, kernel 7.1.9-200.fc44.x86_64, KDE Plasma Wayland session
- Code read and quoted from `main` at `fb1cb4fa6ea4`; also present in `v6.1.0`,

title: podman inspect of a name that matches nothing acquires the lock of every container

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: triaged
labels.description: Issue has been triaged

body:
### Issue Description

`podman inspect NAME` with no `--type` walks the object types. When the name
matches nothing, it reaches the network stage, and `NetworkInspect`
unconditionally calls `GetContainerNetStatuses`, which iterates every container
and takes each container's lock to read its network status
(`pkg/domain/infra/abi/network.go:292` -> `libpod.(*Container).GetNetworkStatus`,
`libpod/container.go:1486`).

Two consequences:

* A lookup that resolves nothing takes N container locks.
* If any single container's lock is unavailable, `podman inspect` of a
  *nonexistent* name blocks forever — while `podman network ls`, which does not
  touch containers, returns immediately.

Using `podman inspect <tag>` as an image existence check is a common pattern,
and it runs precisely on the miss path, so a single stuck container is enough to
wedge it permanently. See https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/issues/29646 for how the container got stuck.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Have one container whose lock is held and not released (any long-held
   container lock will do).
2. `podman network ls` -> returns immediately.
3. `podman inspect some-name-that-does-not-exist` -> hangs forever.
4. `podman inspect --type image some-name-that-does-not-exist` -> returns
   immediately with rc=125.

### Describe the results you received

Measured with a 15 s timeout; rc=124 means it hung, rc=125 means "no such object":

    podman network ls                       rc=0
    podman image exists MISSING             rc=1
    podman inspect --type image MISSING     rc=125
    podman inspect --type container MISSING rc=125
    podman inspect --type pod MISSING       rc=125
    podman inspect --type volume MISSING    rc=125
    podman inspect --type network MISSING   rc=124   <-- hangs
    podman inspect MISSING (no --type)      rc=124   <-- hangs

Goroutine dump of the hanging process (`GOTRACEBACK=all`, then `SIGQUIT`):

    runtime.cgocall
    libpod/lock/shm._Cfunc_lock_semaphore(0x..., 0x4)
    libpod/lock/shm.(*SHMLocks).LockSemaphore(0x..., 0x4)
            libpod/lock/shm/shm_lock.go:227
    libpod/lock.(*SHMLock).Lock(...)
            libpod/lock/shm_lock_manager_linux.go:127
    libpod.(*Container).GetNetworkStatus(...)
            libpod/container.go:1486
    pkg/domain/infra/abi.(*ContainerEngine).GetContainerNetStatuses(...)
            pkg/domain/infra/abi/network.go:292
    pkg/domain/infra/abi.(*ContainerEngine).NetworkInspect(...)
            pkg/domain/infra/abi/network.go:72
    cmd/podman/inspect.(*inspector).inspect(...)
            cmd/podman/inspect/inspect.go:137
    cmd/podman/inspect.Inspect(...)
            cmd/podman/inspect/inspect.go:46

Note that semaphore 4 belongs to a container entirely unrelated to the name
being looked up, and that the requested network does not exist either.

### Describe the results you expected

Resolving a name that matches nothing should not require locking unrelated
containers. A network inspect that fails to find the network should not
enumerate container network statuses at all, and even on success it should not
need every container's lock just to answer "does this network exist".

title: podman run --rm can deadlock with its own `container cleanup`, permanently wedging the per-UID SHM lock

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

body:
### Issue Description

A rootless `podman run --rm` deadlocked with the `podman container cleanup`
process that conmon spawns on container exit. The parent `run` holds the
container's SHM semaphore and waits for its child to finish; the cleanup child
waits for that same semaphore. Neither ever exits.

Because `/dev/shm/libpod_rootless_lock_<uid>` is shared by every rootless podman
invocation of that UID — across all `CONTAINERS_STORAGE_CONF` storages — the
wedged semaphore is not contained to the affected container. Every later podman
command that needs any container lock then blocks forever, including commands
that are not about containers at all (`podman ps -a`, `podman info`, and
`podman inspect NAME` when NAME does not exist).

One deadlocked container blocked an automated build pipeline for six weeks.
Every new run added another permanently hung podman process; 13 had accumulated
by the time it was diagnosed. Meanwhile `podman version`, `podman images`,
`podman network ls` and `podman image exists` kept working normally, which made
the failure look like a storage problem rather than a lock problem.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

Not reproducible on demand — it is a race in the cleanup path. It happened once
under sustained load: a few hundred `podman run --rm` invocations per day over
roughly six weeks, several concurrent at a time, sharing one UID across several
`CONTAINERS_STORAGE_CONF` storages.

1. Run `podman run --rm <image> <command>` repeatedly and concurrently as a
   rootless user.
2. Occasionally one invocation never exits: the container has finished, conmon
   sits in `do_wait`, and the `podman container cleanup --stopped-only --rm <cid>`
   child is blocked on a futex.
3. From then on, every podman command of that UID that touches container locks
   hangs indefinitely, in any storage, until the stuck process is killed.

### Describe the results you received

Process tree at capture, elapsed 1 day 12 h. The shell that started the run had
already been SIGKILLed by an external supervisor, so the top of the chain is
reparented to init while the podman processes stayed alive:

    PID      PPID     WCHAN             CMD
    3514586  1        -                 <login shell>
    3514705  3514586  -                 <wrapper script>
    3530915  3514705  -                 <wrapper script>
    3531787  3530915  -                 <wrapper script>
    3568436  3531787  futex_wait_queue  podman run --rm -v <dir>:<dir> <image> sh -c "<command>"
    3569532  1        do_wait           conmon --api-version 1 -c <cid> -r /usr/bin/runc ... --exit-command podman ... container cleanup --stopped-only --rm <cid>
    3574622  3569532  futex_wait_queue  podman ... container cleanup --stopped-only --rm <cid>

The SHM segment shows semaphore 4 held by a **live** owner. The bitmap at
offset 0x38 is 0x11 (semaphores 0 and 4 allocated); `locks[n]` sits at
`0x40 + 40n`, so `locks[4]` is at offset 0xe0:

    $ dd if=/dev/shm/libpod_rootless_lock_1001 bs=1 skip=224 count=4 | od -An -tu4
    lock word        = 0x8036733d
    owner TID        = 3568445   -> /proc/3568436/task/3568445 (the parent `podman run`)
    FUTEX_WAITERS    = 1
    FUTEX_OWNER_DIED = 0

Every mutex in the segment has `__kind = 0x290`, so `PTHREAD_MUTEX_ROBUST` is
set — but robust recovery never fires, because the owner is alive, merely
blocked.

The three processes wait on different things, which closes the cycle. Comparing
each process's futex addresses against its own mapping of the SHM segment:

    PID 3574622 (container cleanup)
      mapping   7a6c083f8000-7a6c0840d000  /dev/shm/libpod_rootless_lock_1001
      futex     0x7a6c083f80e0             -> offset 0xe0 == locks[4]
      => waiting for semaphore 4

    PID 3568436 (podman run --rm, the recorded owner of semaphore 4)
      mapping   7f2326e12000-7f2326e27000  /dev/shm/libpod_rootless_lock_1001
      futexes   0xc000... and 0x2ed.../0x2ef...   (Go heap and runtime only)
      => NOT waiting on the segment: it holds semaphore 4 and is blocked in the
         Go runtime, waiting for its child to finish

    PID 3569532 (conmon)
      no futex; WCHAN = do_wait
      => waiting for the cleanup child it spawned

So: `podman run --rm` holds semaphore 4 and waits for conmon's child; conmon
waits for `container cleanup`; `container cleanup` waits for semaphore 4.

An unrelated, freshly started podman confirms where waiters pile up
(`GOTRACEBACK=all`, then `SIGQUIT`):

    runtime.cgocall
    libpod/lock/shm._Cfunc_lock_semaphore(0x..., 0x4)
    libpod/lock/shm.(*SHMLocks).LockSemaphore(0x..., 0x4)
            libpod/lock/shm/shm_lock.go:227
    libpod/lock.(*SHMLock).Lock(...)
            libpod/lock/shm_lock_manager_linux.go:127
    libpod.(*Container).GetNetworkStatus(...)
            libpod/container.go:1486
    pkg/domain/infra/abi.(*ContainerEngine).GetContainerNetStatuses(...)
            pkg/domain/infra/abi/network.go:292
    pkg/domain/infra/abi.(*ContainerEngine).NetworkInspect(...)
            pkg/domain/infra/abi/network.go:72
    cmd/podman/inspect.(*inspector).inspect(...)
            cmd/podman/inspect/inspect.go:137
    cmd/podman/inspect.Inspect(...)
            cmd/podman/inspect/inspect.go:46

Measured behaviour of a fresh podman while that one container lock is wedged
(15 s timeout; rc=124 means it hung, rc=125 means "no such object"):

    podman version                          rc=0
    podman images                           rc=0
    podman network ls                       rc=0
    podman image exists MISSING             rc=1
    podman inspect --type image MISSING     rc=125
    podman inspect --type container MISSING rc=125
    podman inspect --type pod MISSING       rc=125
    podman inspect --type volume MISSING    rc=125
    podman inspect --type network MISSING   rc=124   <-- hangs
    podman inspect MISSING (no --type)      rc=124   <-- hangs
    podman ps -a                            rc=124   <-- hangs
    podman info                             rc=124   <-- hangs

`podman info` produces no output and no error message at all — it simply never
returns. Note that this is the one command this bug report form requires, so
while the lock is wedged the required diagnostics cannot be collected.

Killing the lock owner (`kill -9` on the `podman run --rm` process alone) was
enough to resolve everything, and the recovery path behaved exactly as it
should:

    $ kill -9 3568436 ; sleep 5
    lock word        = 0x00000000
    owner TID        = 0
    FUTEX_OWNER_DIED = 0
    $ ps -p 3569532,3574622    # conmon and container cleanup
    (both gone)

The kernel set `FUTEX_OWNER_DIED` on semaphore 4, the waiting `container
cleanup` woke with `EOWNERDEAD`, marked the mutex consistent, finished removing
the container and exited on its own; conmon followed. All queued commands
drained, and `podman info` then reported `freeLocks: 2047`.

In other words the robust-mutex machinery works correctly — nothing is
corrupted, and no `podman system renumber` was needed. The bug is purely the
wait cycle between `run --rm`, conmon and `container cleanup`: as long as all
three stay alive, nothing can break it.

### Describe the results you expected

1. `podman run --rm` and the `container cleanup` process it spawns should not be
   able to deadlock on the same container lock.

2. A container stuck in that state should not be able to block unrelated podman
   invocations of the same UID indefinitely. A bounded wait, or an option in the
   spirit of `--lock-timeout`, would turn a permanent outage into a command that
   fails with a clear message. As it stands there is no diagnostic at all: the
   command simply never returns and never prints anything.

### podman info output

    backend: netavark

### Additional environment details

v5.8.0, commit 07efc23e05c3d9aa15a0f30d57194737bfc4b6b1, Go 1.24.2.
Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8.0-124-generic, x86_64, bare metal.

mount program), runtime runc 1.3.3, DB backend sqlite, network backend
netavark 1.11.0, cgroup manager systemd, conmon 2.1.12, buildah 1.43.0.

Several independent `CONTAINERS_STORAGE_CONF` files are used by the same UID for
different workloads. Note that this does *not* isolate them: the SHM lock
segment is per-UID, so a container wedged in one storage blocks podman in all of
them.


### Additional information

Happens only occasionally — once in roughly six weeks of continuous load. The
host had not been rebooted since before the incident (uptime 78 days) and
lingering is enabled for the user in question, so the runtime directory was
never recreated underneath the running processes.

The supervisor that drives these runs kills a job's shell with SIGKILL on
timeout, which leaves the podman process tree orphaned but alive. That is how
the deadlocked processes survived for six weeks unnoticed.

What made this hard to diagnose is that the failure is completely silent. No
error, no log line, no timeout — affected commands just never return, and the
commands that do work (`version`, `images`, `network ls`, `image exists`) make
the storage look perfectly healthy.

title: fix: specgen: do not inherit image USER with --userns=keep-id
body:
## Problem
When running an image that defines a `USER`, `podman run --userns=keep-id` incorrectly keeps using the image-defined user instead of running the container process as the invoking host user.

## Solution
Modified `pkg/specgen/generate/container.go` to skip populating `s.User` from the image configuration when `s.UserNS.NSMode == specgen.KeepID`. This preserves the fact that no explicit `--user` was passed, allowing `namespaceOptions()` to accurately apply the `keep-id` UID mapping.

Fixes: #29600

## Testing
- Added an e2e test `podman --userns=keep-id overrides image USER` in `test/e2e/run_userns_test.go`.
- All tests passed cleanly.

title: test/e2e: do not use os.Exit for error handling
body:
another item off #18540, "do not use os.Exit() as error handling, let ginkgo handle errors so it can provide useful output".

there were six of them. os.Exit(1) takes the process down before ginkgo can report anything, so what you get in CI is a suite that stops with no failure and no location. three are inside It blocks in top_test.go and trust_test.go, the other three are in the SynchronizedBeforeSuite and in GetPortLock, which also run under ginkgo, so Expect works in all six:

```go
-		user, err := user.Current()
-		if err != nil {
-			os.Exit(1)
-		}
+		user, err := user.Current()
+		Expect(err).ToNot(HaveOccurred())
```

the two in the SynchronizedBeforeSuite were already printing to GinkgoWriter before exiting, so those lose nothing, Expect prints the same error plus the line.

the os.Exit(m.Run()) in TestMain is left alone, that one is how a Go test binary is supposed to exit.

title: bindings: use a per-test network config dir, allow parallel
body:
the epic at #18540 has an item for running the bindings tests in parallel, so I had a look at what was blocking it.

almost everything is already per test. runPodman passes --root, --runroot and --tmpdir from a fresh temp dir, so containers, pods, volumes and images are isolated per service. networks are not, and they should not be, the config dir is shared so podman can keep subnet allocation consistent across services.

what that leaves is two describes that do global network operations. the BeforeEach in networks_test.go prunes unfiltered, and system.Prune prunes networks too:

```go
// Remove all unused networks.
networkPruneOptions := entities.NetworkPruneOptions{}
```

both would take out networks belonging to another test under -p, so they are marked serial the way test/e2e already marks its own network prune test. nothing else in the suite touches networks, and only one It ever creates one.

then -p is gated on GINKGO_PARALLEL the same way ginkgo-run does, so GINKGO_PARALLEL=n puts it back to serial like pkg/machine/e2e.

I could not run the suite locally, I am on macos, so this needs CI.

title: podman image rm - concurrent with shared layers: build fails unpacking its own layer
body:
`podman image rm - concurrent with shared layers` has gone red 9 times between 2026-06-08 and 2026-08-12, on five different distro and mode combinations, so it does not look environmental:

```
5x  int local root fedora-rawhide
1x  int local rootless fedora-rawhide
1x  int local rootless fedora-current
1x  int local rootless debian-sid
1x  int remote root debian-sid
```

The failure is in the build half of the test, not the removal half. The assert that fires is `buildImage()` in common_test.go, and the reason is only on stderr, so the TAP line alone shows a build that ran to COMMIT and exited 1:

```
Error: committing container for step {... Args:[touch rmtest:0] ...}: copying layers and
metadata for container "04c35a38...": writing blob: adding layer with blob "sha256:724a7a77...":
unpacking failed (error: exit status 1; output: open /rmtest:0: no such file or directory)
```

`unpacking failed` comes from `invokeUnpack` in c/storage `pkg/chrootarchive/archive_unix.go`, and the quoted output is what the `storage-untar` re-exec child printed. The child gets the destination as an fd (`/proc/self/fd/4`) and creates entries under it, so an ENOENT while creating `/rmtest:0` reads like the destination went away underneath it rather than the tar being wrong. The test starts ten builds in goroutines off the same base image, which is what makes it concurrent.

The job had composefs and partial images on:

```
--storage-opt overlay.use_composefs=true
--pull-option=enable_partial_images=true --pull-option=convert_images=true
```

I have not reproduced it locally, and I did not get further than the error above, so I do not know which side removes the directory.

#18659 covered the same test being racy but is closed and locked, and that one was about the removal half.

title: test/e2e: remove line matching helpers
body:
picking up one of the open points from #18540, the line matching helpers that only return a bool. when one of these fails all you get is "Expected false to be true", the output that did not match is nowhere in the report.

one commit per helper, same as the earlier LineInOutputStartsWith and ErrorGrepString removals:

GrepString - the callers matched a bool and then indexed into the returned lines. now a single matcher on the output array, so a failure prints every line and the pattern:

```
Expect(run.OutputToStringArray()).To(ContainElement(MatchRegexp(`shm on /dev/shm type tmpfs.*size=10240k`)))
```

LineInOutputContains - both users are plain if conditions, strings.Contains does the same without a helper.

LineInOutputContainsTag - repo/tag lookup in a parsed map, replaced with a line regex. dynamic names go through regexp.QuoteMeta. tagOutputToMap had no other user so it goes too.

I left IsJSONOutputValid alone on purpose, the two users are table tests with an expected bool and BeValidJSON() returns an error instead of a mismatch for invalid json, so ToNot() would blow up on the negative rows.

ran the test/utils suite with goecho built, ok in 4.7s, and golangci-lint with the ci tags is clean.
